title: Physics-Guided Linear Mapper for Quantum Error Mitigation
authors: Tulsi Chaudhari, Krishna Bhatia, Shalini Devendrababu, Srinjoy Ganguly, Luis Gerardo Ayala Bertel
abstract: We introduce a novel physics-guided linear mapper (PGLM) for quantum error mitigation that uses seven distinct interpretable features derived from circuit complexity and device calibration data. The goal is to provide a data-efficient, interpretable, and low-latency alternative to the black-box machine learning for quantum error mitigation in noisy-intermediate scale quantum devices. Evaluated on 52 simulated benchmark circuits (1--4 qubits), PGLM demonstrates strong performance in noise-accumulation regimes: 50.1% RMSE reduction on 3-qubit circuits and 32.3% on 4-qubit circuits, while single-qubit circuits show degraded performance. A circuit-size-aware deployment policy achieves 32.6% aggregate improvement. Sub-millisecond inference enables integration into variational algorithms, and analysis of learned coefficients reveals that circuit depth and CNOT count dominate error prediction, consistent with decoherence mechanisms. Results are simulator-based with idealized noise models; hardware validation remains essential future work.
summary: This paper introduces the Physics-Guided Linear Mapper (PGLM), a novel, low-latency technique for Quantum Error Mitigation in NISQ devices. PGLM uses a linear model trained on circuit-derived features to estimate ideal quantum expectation values from noisy measurements. It proves highly effective in multi-qubit circuits where noise accumulates, offering a practical alternative to black-box machine learning methods.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of Quantum Error Mitigation (QEM) in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices to extract accurate results without full Quantum Error Correction.
main_result: The proposed Physics-Guided Linear Mapper (PGLM) achieves significant RMSE reductions (e.g., 50.1% on 3-qubit circuits) in noise-accumulation regimes while maintaining sub-millisecond inference speed.
method: PGLM uses a linear regression model trained on a minimal, 7-dimensional feature space derived from physical circuit properties (like depth and CNOT count) to map noisy expectation values to ideal ones.
model_or_system: The study simulates quantum circuits on NISQ devices, focusing on 1-to-4 qubit systems subjected to idealized noise models, including depolarizing noise and readout errors.
key_observables: Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) reduction, ideal vs. noisy expectation values, and the performance of the linear mapping coefficients.
important_parameters: Circuit depth, CNOT count, gate error ($p_{	ext{gate}}$), and the regularization parameter ($\alpha$) used in ridge regression.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that error accumulation can be modeled by a linear combination of physically derived features; performance is limited in high-fidelity, single-qubit regimes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the PGLM workflow, comparing raw noisy measurements against the ideal values, and showing performance degradation when moving from multi-qubit to single-qubit circuits.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the PGLM framework, details the physics-guided feature engineering process, presents the training methodology using ridge regression, and evaluates performance across varying circuit complexities and noise regimes.
why_interesting: The focus on data-efficient, physically interpretable ML techniques for noise mitigation is highly relevant for developing practical quantum algorithms on near-term hardware.
